Do two timed mock interviews out loud

Interview day
Skim the one-page cheat sheet, then stop studying

- **KYC / AML**: Know Your Customer and Anti-Money Laundering. Identity checks and transaction monitoring required by regulators.

- **Chargeback**: Customer-initiated dispute that reverses a card payment.
- **Ledger**: Source-of-truth record of balances and transactions; double-entry accounting.

## Metrics to know
- **TPV**: Total payment volume
- **Take rate**: Revenue / TPV
- **CAC / LTV**: Customer acquisition cost vs. lifetime value
- **Fraud rate** and **approval rate**
- **NIM**: Net interest margin (lending)

# Handy phrases

- **Hello** – Konnichiwa
- **Thank you** – Arigatou gozaimasu
- **Excuse me / Sorry** – Sumimasen
- **Please** – Onegaishimasu
- **How much is it?** – Ikura desu ka?
- **Where is the toilet?** – Toire wa doko desu ka?
- **I'm allergic to…** – ...arerugii ga arimasu
- **Delicious!** – Oishii!
- **Check, please** – Okaikei onegaishimasu
- **One more, please** – Moo hitotsu kudasai

## Etiquette reminders
- No tipping
- Don't eat while walking
- Keep voices low on trains
- Take shoes off where required
- Carry small trash with you; bins are scarce

# Project Brief: Migrating the Team Wiki to PlexiiWrite

## Purpose

This brief sets out why and how we will move our team wiki into PlexiiWrite. It is meant to give everyone involved a shared understanding of the goals, what is and is not included, the rough sequence of work, and the main risks to manage. It is a first draft and should be edited as decisions are made.

## Goals

The aim is to have one reliable, current home for team knowledge in PlexiiWrite, with the old wiki retired once the move is complete. Success means:

- All pages we choose to keep are available in PlexiiWrite with their content, structure and links intact.
- Team members know where to find things and are editing in PlexiiWrite rather than the old wiki.
- Outdated or duplicate pages are removed or archived rather than carried over by default.
- The old wiki is set to read-only and then decommissioned on an agreed date.

[Add the main reason for the move, for example cost, search quality, or consolidating tools, so the goals have a clear motivation.]

## Scope

In scope are the content audit, the decision on what to keep, archive or delete, the import or manual transfer of retained pages, the structure and naming conventions for the new space, permissions setup, link and attachment checks, and a short orientation for the team.

Out of scope for this project are rewriting content beyond what is needed to fix broken formatting, building integrations with other tools, and any changes to how the team works outside the wiki. If any of these turn out to matter, they should be raised as separate work.

Open questions to settle early: [current wiki platform and approximate page count], [whether PlexiiWrite offers an import tool for our current format or the move must be done manually], and [who has final say on what is archived].

## Roles

- Project owner: [owner name], accountable for delivery and the final cutover decision.
- Content leads: [names], responsible for reviewing their areas of the wiki and deciding what to keep.
- Admin for PlexiiWrite: [name], responsible for workspace setup, permissions and access.
- Team members: review pages in their area and adopt the new space.

## Timeline

Dates are to be confirmed. The work follows five phases, and each should have an end date once the owner and leads agree capacity.

1. Audit and planning. Inventory existing pages, flag what to keep, archive or delete, and agree the new structure. Target: [date].
2. Workspace setup. Create the space, set permissions, and define templates and naming conventions. Target: [date].
3. Pilot migration. Move one section end to end, check formatting, links and attachments, and adjust the approach. Target: [date].
4. Full migration. Transfer the remaining retained content, with content leads checking their areas. Target: [date].
5. Cutover and wrap-up. Announce the switch, set the old wiki to read-only, run a short orientation, and decommission the old wiki on [date].

## Risks

- Content is migrated that nobody needs, which clutters the new space. To reduce this, require an explicit keep decision during the audit instead of moving everything.
- Formatting, internal links or attachments break in transfer. The pilot phase exists to find these issues early, and each content lead should spot-check their pages.
- Team members keep using the old wiki, leaving two sources of truth. Set a clear read-only date, communicate it early, and name the owner of the new space.
- Permissions are set up incorrectly, exposing sensitive pages or blocking access. Review access with the admin before full migration.
- Work stalls because content leads lack time. Agree expected effort up front and confirm it with their managers.
- Information is lost when the old wiki is shut down. Keep a backup or export of the old wiki for an agreed period before deletion.

## Next Steps

Confirm the project owner and content leads, answer the open questions in the scope section, and schedule the audit so the dates above can be filled in.

groundingDetail.original:
# Support Agent Onboarding Guide

## Welcome

Welcome to the team. This guide covers what to expect in your first week, the tools you will use every day, and how we handle escalations. Read it through once before your first day, then keep it open as a reference. Anything marked in [square brackets] is a detail your manager or buddy will fill in or confirm with you.

Your goal for week one is not speed. It is to understand our customers, learn where to find answers, and know exactly when and how to ask for help. Speed follows from that.

## Who to go to

You will have a few named people to lean on in your first weeks.

- Your manager is [manager name]. They own your goals, schedule, and feedback.
- Your onboarding buddy is [buddy name]. Ask them anything, including the questions that feel too small to ask anyone else.
- For escalations and technical questions, the on-call or escalation contact is [name or rotation].
- For access, accounts, and equipment problems, contact [IT or ops contact].

Our team chat channel is [channel name]. Use it for quick questions, and post there before you spend more than [time, e.g. 15 minutes] stuck on something.

## Your first week

The plan below is a suggested shape. Your manager will confirm the real schedule and any meetings.

### Day one: get set up and get oriented

Spend the day on access, introductions, and the big picture. Confirm that you can log in to every tool listed in the next section. Meet your manager and buddy, and join the team channels. Read through our product overview and our support principles at [link to documents]. By the end of the day you should be able to explain in a couple of sentences what our product does and who uses it.

### Days two and three: shadow and learn

Sit in on live work with your buddy, either in person or by screen share. Watch how they read a ticket, search for answers, write a reply, and decide whether to escalate. Read a sample of recently solved tickets, including a few that were escalated, and notice how the replies are written. Start working through the knowledge base, focusing on the topics that make up most of our volume, which your buddy can point out.

### Day four: handle tickets with a safety net

Begin answering real tickets in a supervised mode. Your buddy or manager reviews your replies before they are sent, or immediately after, depending on [team review process]. Expect plenty of feedback. It is a normal part of learning the work, not a judgment of you.

### Day five: reflect and set goals

Work a small queue on your own, with review afterward. Close the week with a one-on-one with your manager to talk about what felt clear, what did not, and what to focus on in weeks two through four. Come with three questions and one thing you think we could document better.

## Tools you will use

You will work in a handful of systems. Your manager will confirm access for each.

- The helpdesk, [helpdesk tool], is where every customer conversation lives. You will use it to read tickets, reply, tag, assign, and escalate.
- The knowledge base, [knowledge base tool], holds our help articles and internal answers. Search here first, and flag anything that is wrong or missing.
- Team chat, [chat tool], is for questions, handoffs, and incident announcements.
- The admin or account lookup tool, [admin tool], lets you view a customer's account and settings. Access is limited to what you need, and customer data should only be viewed when a ticket requires it.
- The bug or issue tracker, [tracker tool], is where product problems are logged and where you can check whether an issue is already known.
- Our status page, [status page link], shows current incidents. Check it when several customers report the same problem.

Keep a personal list of the links, saved replies, and search terms you use most. It will save you time every day.

## How we handle a ticket

Most tickets can and should be resolved by you. A good response does a few things consistently.

1. Read the whole conversation, including earlier tickets and internal notes, before replying.
2. Work out what the customer actually needs, which is not always what they first asked.
3. Check the knowledge base and the tracker for known answers and known issues.
4. Reply in plain, friendly language. Acknowledge the problem, give the answer or next step, and say what will happen next and when.
5. Tag the ticket correctly so we can spot trends.
6. Set the status honestly. Do not close a ticket unless the problem is solved or the customer has what they need.

Our response targets are [first response target] for first reply and [resolution target] for resolution, and they may vary by [plan or priority]. If you are at risk of missing one, tell your buddy or manager early rather than late.

## How we handle escalations

Escalating is a normal and expected part of the job. It is not a failure, and it is far better than guessing. The aim is to get the customer to the right person quickly, with enough information that nobody has to ask them to repeat themselves.

### When to escalate

Escalate when a ticket falls into one of these situations. The exact thresholds are set by the team, so confirm them with your manager: [thresholds and criteria].

- The customer reports a possible bug that you can reproduce or that matches a pattern across tickets.
- Multiple customers report the same problem, which may indicate an outage.
- The issue involves security, privacy, or a possible exposure of customer data.
- The request involves a refund, credit, or exception beyond your authority of [your authority limit].
- The customer mentions legal action, a regulator, or the press.
- The customer is distressed or very upset and the conversation is not improving.
- You have worked on the problem for [time limit] and are not making progress.
- You are unsure, and getting it wrong would be costly for the customer.

Security and data concerns should be escalated immediately through [urgent escalation channel], not left in the queue.

### Escalation levels

We handle escalations in tiers.

- Tier one is you and the rest of the front-line team. Ask your buddy or post in [channel] for a second opinion.
- Tier two is [tier two team or person], who handle complex technical and account issues.
- Tier three is [engineering or product contact], who handle confirmed bugs and incidents through [process].
- For urgent incidents, the contact is [incident owner or on-call rotation].

### What to include in a handoff

A good escalation lets the next person start working immediately. Include the following in the ticket or escalation form at [link or template].

- A one-line summary of the problem and its impact on the customer.
- The customer's account details and relevant plan, with a link to the ticket.
- The exact steps to reproduce the problem, or what you have seen so far.
- What you have already tried and what the result was.
- Any screenshots, error messages, or logs.
- How urgent it is and why.
- What you have told the customer, and what you have promised about timing.

### Staying in touch with the customer

Escalating does not mean stepping away. Tell the customer that you are bringing in a colleague, set honest expectations about timing, and follow up at the interval we have agreed of [update interval]. Stay the customer's point of contact unless the ticket has been formally reassigned. Do not promise a fix date unless the team that owns the fix has confirmed it.

### After the escalation

When the issue is resolved, read how it was handled. Update the ticket, add to the knowledge base if the answer will help others, and ask yourself whether you could have solved it next time. Your manager may review escalations with you in your one-on-ones. The point is to learn, not to assign blame.

## What good looks like

In your first month, we are looking for a few things more than raw numbers. Aim for accurate answers, a warm and clear tone, careful tagging, honest status updates, and a habit of asking early. Your manager will share the specific quality measures and targets we use at [link or meeting], and how your work will be reviewed.

## First-week checklist

- [ ] I have

The knowledge base, [knowledge base tool], holds our help articles and internal answers. Search here first, and flag anything that is wrong or missing.
Team chat, [chat tool], is for questions, handoffs, and incident announcements.
The admin or account lookup tool, [admin tool], lets you view a customer's account and settings. Access is limited to what you need, and customer data should only be viewed when a ticket requires it.
The bug or issue tracker, [tracker tool], is where product problems are logged and where you can check whether an issue is already known.
Our status page, [status page link], shows current incidents. Check it when several customers report the same problem.
Keep a personal list of the links, saved replies, and search terms you use most. It will save you time every day.
How we handle a ticket
Most tickets can and should be resolved by you. A good response does a few things consistently.
Read the whole conversation, including earlier tickets and internal notes, before replying.
Work out what the customer actually needs, which is not always what they first asked.
Check the knowledge base and the tracker for known answers and known issues.
Reply in plain, friendly language. Acknowledge the problem, give the answer or next step, and say what will happen next and when.
Tag the ticket correctly so we can spot trends.
Set the status honestly. Do not close a ticket unless the problem is solved or the customer has what they need.

Our response targets are [first response target] for first reply and [resolution target] for resolution, and they may vary by [plan or priority]. If you are at risk of missing one, tell your buddy or manager early rather than late.
How we handle escalations

Escalating is a normal and expected part of the job. It is not a failure, and it is far better than guessing. The aim is to get the customer to the right person quickly, with enough information that nobody has to ask them to repeat themselves.
When to escalate
Escalate when a ticket falls into one of these situations. The exact thresholds are set by the team, so confirm them with your manager: [thresholds and criteria].
The customer reports a possible bug that you can reproduce or that matches a pattern across tickets.
Multiple customers report the same problem, which may indicate an outage.
The issue involves security, privacy, or a possible exposure of customer data.
The request involves a refund, credit, or exception beyond your authority of [your authority limit].
The customer mentions legal action, a regulator, or the press.
The customer is distressed or very upset and the conversation is not improving.
You have worked on the problem for [time limit] and are not making progress.
You are unsure, and getting it wrong would be costly for the customer.
Security and data concerns should be escalated immediately through [urgent escalation channel], not left in the queue.
Escalation levels
We handle escalations in tiers.
Tier one is you and the rest of the front-line team. Ask your buddy or post in [channel] for a second opinion.
Tier two is [tier two team or person], who handle complex technical and account issues.
Tier three is [engineering or product contact], who handle confirmed bugs and incidents through [process].
For urgent incidents, the contact is [incident owner or on-call rotation].
What to include in a handoff
A good escalation lets the next person start working immediately. Include the following in the ticket or escalation form at [link or template].
A one-line summary of the problem and its impact on the customer.
The customer's account details and relevant plan, with a link to the ticket.
The exact steps to reproduce the problem, or what you have seen so far.
What you have already tried and what the result was.
Any screenshots, error messages, or logs.
How urgent it is and why.
What you have told the customer, and what you have promised about timing.
Staying in touch with the customer

Escalating does not mean stepping away. Tell the customer that you are bringing in a colleague, set honest expectations about timing, and follow up at the interval we have agreed of [update interval]. Stay the customer's point of contact unless the ticket has been formally reassigned. Do not promise a fix date unless the team that owns the fix has confirmed it.
After the escalation

When the issue is resolved, read how it was handled. Update the ticket, add to the knowledge base if the answer will help others, and ask yourself whether you could have solved it next time. Your manager may review escalations with you in your one-on-ones. The point is to learn, not to assign blame.
What good looks like

In your first month, we are looking for a few things more than raw numbers. Aim for accurate answers, a warm and clear tone, careful tagging, honest status updates, and a habit of asking early. slides.title: How to Write a Good Bug Report
slides.notes: Welcome everyone. By the end of this session you will know what a useful bug report contains and how to write one in a few minutes. The goal is simple: the person who picks up your report should be able to act on it without chasing you for details.

slides.title: Why report quality matters
bullets: A vague report forces the reader to guess or ask follow-up questions
Every round of back and forth delays the fix
Bugs that cannot be reproduced are often closed or ignored
A clear report lets the right person start work immediately
Good reports also become a useful record of what went wrong
slides.notes: Start with the cost of a bad report. If the developer cannot reproduce the problem, they have to stop and ask you, and the bug sits waiting. A few extra minutes from you saves much more time on the other side.

slides.title: The anatomy of a good report
bullets: A short, specific title that names the problem
Steps to reproduce, numbered and in order
Expected result and actual result, stated separately
Environment: version, device, browser, operating system
Evidence: screenshot, recording, logs or error text
Severity and who or what is affected
slides.notes: Walk through each part and explain why it is there. The title helps people scan the backlog, the steps let them see it for themselves, and the expected versus actual comparison shows why it counts as a bug. Environment and evidence save the most guessing.

slides.title: Writing steps that others can follow
bullets: Start from a known state, such as a fresh login
One action per step, written in plain words
Include the exact data or input you used
Say whether it happens every time or only sometimes
Remove steps that are not needed to trigger the bug
Test your own steps once before submitting
slides.notes: Steps are the heart of the report. Write them as if the reader has never seen this part of the product. If the bug is intermittent, say so and note anything you noticed about when it happens. Running through your own steps once catches missing details.

slides.title: Weak report versus strong report
bullets: Weak title: Search is broken
Strong title: Search returns no results when the query contains an apostrophe
Weak body: It did not work when I tried it
Strong body: numbered steps, expected result, actual result, version and a screenshot
Weak tone: blame or frustration
Strong tone: neutral, factual and specific
slides.notes: Use this slide to make the difference concrete. Read the weak title aloud and ask the room what questions it raises. Then show how the strong version answers them before anyone has to ask. Keep the tone factual, since the report is about the product and not about a person.

slides.title: Before you hit submit
bullets: Search for an existing report and add to it if you find one
Check that the title makes sense on its own
Confirm steps, expected result and actual result are all present
Attach evidence and note the environment
Report one problem per ticket
Watch for follow-up questions and reply promptly
slides.notes: Finish with a checklist people can use every time. Encourage them to keep it nearby for their next report. Remind them that a good report is a small piece of teamwork, and invite questions before we close. If there is a team template or tracker link, add it here: [link to bug report template].
